name: The Ventriloquist Effect
statement: We hear a sound as coming from wherever we see its likely source, so the voice seems to come from the moving puppet.
statementAccent: the voice seems to come from the moving puppet
meaning: The ventriloquist effect is a multisensory perceptual illusion in which the perceived location of a sound is shifted toward a simultaneous visual stimulus, so that vision captures or dominates the localisation of sound. It is named after the stage act of ventriloquism, where a performer keeps their own lips still while moving the puppet's mouth, and the voice seems to come from the puppet rather than from the performer. The same effect operates everywhere: in a cinema or watching television, the dialogue seems to come from the actors' mouths on screen even though the sound actually issues from speakers to the side. The effect arises because the brain integrates the seen and heard signals, and because vision usually has better spatial resolution than hearing, the visual location generally wins. It is a classic demonstration of multisensory integration and cross-modal perception in cognitive science.
mechanism: When audio and visual signals occur close together in time and space, the brain tends to treat them as arising from a single event and binds them together, then estimates the location by combining the two senses. Crucially, the combination is weighted by reliability: because vision typically localises objects more precisely than hearing, the visual estimate dominates, pulling the perceived sound location toward the seen source. This is not blind visual dominance but near-optimal integration, as shown by experiments in which degrading the visual signal, for instance by blurring it, reduces its weight and can even let sound capture vision. Over time, repeated exposure to a consistent spatial mismatch between where a sound is and where it is seen produces the ventriloquism aftereffect, a lasting recalibration of sound localisation that persists even when the visual stimulus is removed. The everyday experience of hearing speech come from a talker's visible mouth, or dialogue from on-screen actors, is the effect operating in real time.

examples.text: A ventriloquist keeps their lips still and moves the puppet's mouth, so the audience hears the voice as coming from the puppet, not the performer.
In a theatre, dialogue seems to come from the actors' mouths on screen even though the sound actually comes from speakers spread around the room.
After repeated exposure to a consistent audio-visual spatial mismatch, sound localisation is recalibrated and stays shifted even without the visual stimulus.

variants.name: Reliability-weighted integration
variants.text: The account that the brain combines the seen and heard locations weighted by their reliability, so the more precise sense, usually vision, dominates.

variants.name: The ventriloquism aftereffect
variants.text: The lasting recalibration of sound localisation produced by repeated exposure to a spatial audio-visual mismatch, persisting after the visual cue is gone.

whyItMatters: The ventriloquist effect is a classic demonstration of multisensory integration, showing how the brain fuses information from different senses into a single, coherent perception of the world. It reveals that perception is not a matter of each sense working alone but of combining them, weighted by their reliability, so that the more precise sense shapes the outcome, a principle that extends far beyond sound localisation to how the brain resolves conflicting sensory information generally. The effect explains everyday experiences, from the seamless illusion of speech coming from a talker's mouth to dialogue appearing to come from on-screen actors, and it underlies technologies from film sound to virtual and augmented reality, where aligning seen and heard sources is essential for immersion. As a vivid, easily demonstrated instance of vision capturing sound, it has become a cornerstone example in perceptual psychology and cognitive science.

working.lead: Pair a sound with a seen source
working.text: present a sound and a visual stimulus close together in time and space, as with a talker's moving mouth.
have the brain treat them as one event and combine their locations, weighting each by its reliability.
because vision usually localises more precisely, perceive the sound as coming from the seen source, capturing its location.

limits: The ventriloquist effect reflects reliability-weighted integration rather than absolute visual dominance, so it is not that vision always wins; when the visual signal is unreliable, for example severely blurred, its weight falls and sound can capture vision instead. The effect operates when the seen and heard signals are close enough in time and space to be plausibly bound to one event; large mismatches break the binding and the illusion fails. Its strength varies with the stimuli, the observer, and attention. And while vision tends to dominate spatial judgments, hearing can dominate temporal ones in related illusions, so no single sense is uniformly in charge. The ventriloquist effect thus illustrates a general principle of reliability-weighted multisensory combination rather than a fixed rule that sight overrides sound.
misreadings: The effect is not that we cannot hear where sounds come from; it is that when a plausible visual source is present, the brain shifts the perceived sound location toward it through integration. It is not blind visual dominance either, since an unreliable visual cue loses weight and sound can prevail. And it requires the seen and heard signals to be close enough to be bound as one event, so treating it as vision always overriding hearing, or as working regardless of how mismatched the cues are, misreads a reliability-weighted process with clear conditions.
origin: A classic multisensory illusion named after the ventriloquism act, studied in perceptual psychology as visual capture of sound and shown to reflect near-optimal, reliability-weighted integration of vision and hearing.
